props.own: A more favorable attitude toward a behavior strengthens the intention to perform it.
Stronger perceived expectations from important others strengthen intention.
Greater perceived control over the behavior strengthens intention.
Intention, with perceived control, predicts whether the behavior happens.
Perceived behavioral control also predicts the behavior directly, together with intention.

reasons.c0>med: Veterans who expect therapy to help them value attending, so they plan to keep going.
reasons.c1>med: When spouses, fellow veterans, and clinicians endorse treatment, veterans feel supported in planning to continue.
reasons.c2>med: Veterans who believe they can fit sessions around work, child care, and travel are more likely to plan to stay.
reasons.med>out: A plan to stay in treatment turns into attendance when the opportunity is there.
reasons.c2>out: Veterans who can arrange transportation and time off attend more sessions, even if they did not plan to.
reasons.m0~: Long drives add cost and time to every visit, so intention leads to attendance less often for veterans 30 or more miles away.

state.rq:
Main question: Among post-9/11 U.S. veterans enrolled in VA mental health care, how do attitude toward the behavior, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control relate to treatment engagement?

Subquestions:
1. Does intention to stay in treatment explain these relationships?
2. Does the relationship between intention to stay in treatment and treatment engagement differ by distance to care?

notes.journal: Journal of Human Behavior in the Social Environment
notes.phenomenon: Many post-9/11 veterans who begin VA psychotherapy stop before completing an adequate course of care.
notes.typical: Usually defined as dropout or nonadherence, a property of the individual veteran, because clinics track attendance patient by patient.
notes.alternative: It can be defined as a mismatch between how care is delivered and veterans' lives: distance, work schedules, and military norms about help-seeking. This moves attention from the veteran to the system and makes room for structural explanations alongside individual ones.
notes.need: This example asks whether the theory's individual focus is enough to explain engagement when access barriers such as distance to care are present.

A.ontology: Behavior has causes in a person's beliefs that exist independently of the researcher and can be approximated, though never known perfectly.
A.epistemology: Beliefs, intentions, and behavior can be measured with standardized self-report and records and tested with statistical models.
A.history: Extends Fishbein and Ajzen's theory of reasoned action by adding perceived behavioral control; rooted in expectancy-value models of attitudes.
A.limits: Makes individual beliefs and intentions visible. Structural conditions such as distance to care stay outside the model unless they act through perceived control.
A.practice: Points practice toward changing beliefs and perceived control (motivational interviewing, peer veterans, scheduling and travel support) and policy toward reducing access barriers.
